abstract: This study investigates the proficiency of three leading GPTs, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini, in answering final-exam questions for an undergraduate course in Financial Markets and Intermediaries, a specialized finance education context characterized by heterogeneous cognitive and assessment demands. Drawing on Bloom’s revised taxonomy and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), this study examines whether GPT performance varies across assessment formats requiring different levels of cognitive processing and reasoning. The results revealed significant divergences: Gemini achieved the highest scores, demonstrating strong comprehension and reasoning skills, whereas ChatGPT showed moderate proficiency and DeepSeek underperformed. All models performed better on multiple-choice questions than on open-ended questions, suggesting that GPTs currently perform more effectively in tasks associated with lower-order cognitive processes. Computational questions posed the greatest challenges across all models, supporting theoretical expectations from CLT. The findings contribute to literature on generative AI in higher education showing that GPT proficiency is not uniform across cognitive assessment levels and by proposing a framework linking AI performance to educational assessment theories. Highly proficient GPTs can serve as valuable supplementary tools for students and educators; however, limitations in complex reasoning, computational accuracy, and regulatory interpretation require critical use. Findings should be interpreted with caution given the single-course single-institution setting.

abstract: This paper derives the exact minimum number of impact sign restrictions required to identify shocks in a structural vector autoregression under a natural pairwise separation condition. The answer is . The proof follows from deriving a sharp lower bound using a Kraft-type inequality and then constructing an admissible restriction matrix that attains the bound. Our result reveals a significant sparsity gain: while traditional recursive orderings require restrictions, sign-based separation requires only , providing a transparent benchmark for designing sparse identifying schemes in large SVARs.
title: How many sign restrictions are needed? A sharp lower bound for identifying multiple shocks in SVARs

abstract: This study investigates the impact of government accounting supervision on the adoption of supply chain finance (SCF) among Chinese listed firms. Using a difference‐in‐differences (DID) approach and a comprehensive dataset spanning 1999 to 2022, we find robust evidence that government accounting supervision significantly promotes the adoption of SCF. This relationship remains resilient across a battery of robustness checks, including parallel trend analysis, propensity score matching (PSM‐DID), placebo tests, and alternative sample specifications. Mechanism analysis reveals that the positive impact of government accounting supervision is primarily driven by enhanced supply chain transparency and the suppression of abnormal related‐party transactions. Furthermore, cross‐sectional analyses reveal that this effect is more pronounced in firms with higher supplier concentration or those lacking political connections. Overall, our findings offer important insights into the role of institutional oversight in fostering financial innovation and enhancing supply chain sustainability.

abstract: This paper investigates how informal political patronage subverts environmental regulation and local economic performance in China. We demonstrate that patronage provides local officials with political insurance, enabling them to safely shield polluting firms from top-down enforcement. Contrary to the promotion tournament hypothesis, this forbearance does not drive GDP growth. Instead, it is sustained through localized rent extraction. Utilizing firm-level data and shocks induced by provincial party secretary turnover, we find that connected officials extract a political tax, measured via perk expenditures, from both polluting and non-polluting enterprises. This systemic extortion generates broad negative spillovers: while shielding incumbent polluters, patronage crowds out productive investment and deters clean market entrants, ultimately degrading both environmental outcomes and the regional business environment.

abstract: The year 2025 was unprecedented in the frequency, complexity, and volatility of US trade policy interventions. This column uses a new database tracking US tariff announcements during the year to show that confusion about the current state of tariff policy led to a decline in US imports that was similar in size to the reduction caused by tariff increases alone, meaning that confusion doubled the negative impact of tariffs. Product customisation, relationship trust, and partner reputation can help firms maintain trade activity during information shocks.
authors: Kalina Manova, Dennis Novy, Thomas Sampson, Aaron Tang

abstract: US net migration turned negative in 2025 following a sharp tightening of immigration policies. This column turns to the Age of Mass Migration and the sharp policy reversal of the 1921 and 1924 Quota Acts to examine how immigration shapes long-run growth through its contribution to innovation. The authors find that without the Age of Mass Migration, US GDP per capita would have been 8.2% lower by 1940, while the policy that ended mass migration harmed the US comparatively little. They also demonstrate the importance of geography: the impact of immigration on productivity depends not only on how many arrive and how skilled they are, but also where they settle.
authors: Costas Arkolakis, Sun Kyoung Lee, Michael Peters
title: Immigration, innovation, and the geography of growth: Lessons from the Age of Mass Migration
